title: Looking back: no excuse
hookLine: a discourse we passed: Sariputta tells a brahmin that duty to family does not excuse harming others

lines: I'M DOING IT FOR MY FAMILY.
cards: I'm doing it for my family. People say it about the best things they do, and sometimes about the worst.
In the ninety-seventh discourse, Sariputta hears news of an old acquaintance, a brahmin named Dhananjani who works for the king. He's gotten careless, people say.
He uses the king's authority to squeeze the brahmin householders, and uses the householders as cover to cheat the king. Sariputta goes to find him.

teach.b: He finds him at a cowshed while the cows are being milked. Dhananjani offers fresh milk; Sariputta has already eaten for the day, and asks: Dhananjani, are you diligent? How can I be? the brahmin answers.

teach.h: I HAVE SO MANY TO SUPPORT
teach.b: I have my parents to support. A wife and children. Workers.
Duties to friends, to ancestors, to the gods, to the king. And this body has to be fed too. It's an honest list, and a heavy one.
Sariputta doesn't dismiss it. He asks a question. Suppose a man broke the moral law for his parents' sake, and when he died, the wardens of the hell realms dragged him off.

teach.h: COULD HE SAY: I DID IT FOR THEM?
teach.b: Could he say: I did it for my parents, let me go? Could his parents say: he did it for us, let him go? No, says Dhananjani.
Then the same question for wife and children, workers, friends, ancestors, the gods, the king, this body. No, every time. One more.
Who's better: the one who does wrong for his parents, or the one who does right for them? The one who does right.
Then there are other ways, Sariputta says, in line with the dhamma, to earn a living, support your parents, and do no harm. The Pali word is dhammika: righteous, in keeping with the dhamma.
Family duty isn't the problem; elsewhere the discourses honor it. But love for your own doesn't turn harm to others into something else. The duty stays.

how: Buddhist ethics across schools honors support for parents and family as a duty while holding that right livelihood, earning without harming others, is part of the eightfold path; MN 97 is one place this is spelled out.

o: returning to a discourse we passed by
a review of every lesson so far
regret for the choices you made

p: the brahmin who served the king
no excuse to the wardens of hell
righteous, in line with the dhamma

s: Sariputta tells Dhananjani that supporting his family is a distraction
he never questions the duty; he questions the harm done in its name.
Sariputta turns down the milk because he disapproves of Dhananjani
he says only that he has already eaten for the day.
Dhananjani agrees that doing right for one's parents is better than doing wrong for them
and Sariputta says there are righteous ways to support them.

games.q: you're Sariputta. Dhananjani says: how can I be diligent? I have parents, wife, children, workers, king and gods to look after. what do you do?
o: ask whether harm done for their sake would be excused.
tell him to leave his family and become a monk.
agree that he has no choice.
games.why: Sariputta asks question after question, and Dhananjani sees for himself: the duty is real, but no one can excuse the harm.

practice: Let one excuse you use come up, I'm too busy, everyone does it, it's for the kids, and hold it gently, the way Sariputta held Dhananjani's list. Is the duty real?
Probably; now ask whether there's a way to meet it without the harm, and just see one other way, without solving it all.

wordCard.voice: Looking back. A second discourse we passed: duty to family is real, but it never makes harming others right.

orig.note: Pali dhammika: righteous, in keeping with the dhamma. the other way to support a family.

carryVoice: Your line: no excuse. There's a righteous way to carry the same load. Day five hundred nineteen, done.
